investment_summary:
Equifax grew 2025 revenue 7% to $6,074.5 million and diluted EPS 10% to $5.32 [1]. Operating margin slipped to 18.0%, and the balance sheet is more stretched: a 0.61x current ratio and $1,038.0 million of debt due within a year against $180.8 million of cash [1].

At $185.68, the stock trades at 21.8x FY2026 consensus EPS of $8.50 [2][3]. The reverse DCF is the demanding part: today's enterprise value implies 12.4% annual revenue growth for ten years, against a 5.8% historical three-year CAGR and consensus growth of 9.7% for 2026 and 6.1% for 2027 [2][3]. The implied return of 7.8% sits below the 11.2% WACC. The valuation therefore requires sustained re-acceleration, not a return to recent trend. Consensus data is dated after the 10-K.

Free cash flow of $1,134.3 million covered the $232.8 million dividend, but the $927.5 million of buybacks was partly funded by $474.7 million of commercial paper [1]. Four straight EPS beats are encouraging, but next-year estimates fell 6.3% in 90 days [3].
key_takeaways: USIS margin gains should continue as mortgage pricing holds: operating margin rose to 22.9% from 21.4% [1].
Workforce Solutions should keep anchoring profit despite the mortgage slowdown, because its 44.2% margin is the group's highest [1].
Shares look fully valued: the reverse DCF needs 12.4% annual revenue growth, against 9.7% consensus for 2026 and 5.8% historically [2][3].
Refinancing is the key balance sheet risk: $1,038.0 million of debt is due within a year against $180.8 million of cash [1][2].
business_overview:
Equifax Inc., founded in 1913, is a global data, analytics and technology company that supplies information solutions to businesses, governments and consumers, plus human resources business process outsourcing to employers [1]. Revenue reached $6,074.5 million in 2025, up 7% from $5,681.1 million, and the company reports three segments: Workforce Solutions (43% of revenue), U.S. Information Solutions (USIS, 34%) and International (23%) [1]. The U.S. generated 77% of revenue, with operations in 20 countries outside the U.S. [1]. Strategic priorities include migrating to a public cloud platform and using AI and machine learning to develop products, while capital was returned through $927.4 million of share repurchases and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.50 [1].

Workforce Solutions is the profit anchor. Revenue rose 6% to $2,582.3 million and operating income rose 8% to $1,141.5 million, lifting operating margin to 44.2% from 43.3% [1]. Its core asset, The Work Number, held about 209 million active and 813 million total employment records at year-end, drawn from payroll data of more than 4 million organizations [1]. Verification Services grew 8% to $2,179.8 million, while Employer Services fell 2% to $402.5 million on lower unemployment claims, ACA and I-9 revenue [1]. A Workforce Solutions business acquired in 2025 for $74.1 million net of cash acquired added to the segment [1].

USIS is the fastest-growing segment. Revenue rose 10% to $2,078.5 million and operating income rose 18% to $475.2 million, with margin improving to 22.9% from 21.4% [1]. Online Information Solutions grew 10% to $1,821.4 million, and Financial Marketing Services grew 6% to $257.1 million [1]. International revenue rose 4% to $1,413.7 million (6% in local currency), but operating margin fell to 12.9% from 13.4% on higher people costs and amortization of capitalized internal-use software from earlier technology spending [1]. At the current share price of $185.68, consensus carries a buy rating and a $205.10 target price, implying upside of about 10% [2][3].
market_position:
Equifax does not disclose market share in its 10-K, and it describes competitors only by category: in-house HR teams, payroll processors and global consumer credit reporting companies [1]. Its clients span mortgage, financial services, employers, government, automotive and telecommunications, and the largest client accounts for about 3% of revenue [1]. The filing does not name customers or describe their credit quality, so customer concentration can be assessed only through that single figure [1]. We classify Equifax as a scaled incumbent rather than a challenger: it is the largest company by revenue in the peer set and the filing claims that no competitor offers quite the same mix of products, although it does not quantify that advantage [1][4].

Scale does not translate into the highest margins. Equifax's 2025 revenue of $6,074 million is ahead of Paychex ($5,572 million), TransUnion ($4,576 million) and Verisk ($3,073 million), but its EBITDA margin of 30.2% trails TransUnion's 31.8%, and its gross margin of 56.4% is the lowest of the four [4]. Verisk and Paychex earn far higher EBITDA margins, at 54.3% and 44.7% respectively [4]. Equifax's ROIC of 8.5% is ahead of TransUnion's 6.7% but well behind Verisk's 20.7% and Paychex's 19.1% [4].

Growth is mid-pack. Equifax grew 6.9% in 2025, against TransUnion's 9.4%, Verisk's 6.6% and Paychex's 5.6% [4]. The shares trade at $185.68, about 33% below the 52-week high of $275.92 and 13% above the low of $164.02 [2]. The market position is therefore strong in scale and proprietary employment and credit data, but the margin and return gap to asset-light peers limits how much premium the business can command.
operating_results:
Revenue grew 7% to $6,074.5 million in 2025, after 8% growth in 2024, led by USIS (+10%), while International grew 4% and absorbed a $21.7 million currency drag [1]. Selling, general and administrative expense rose 11% to $1,614.2 million on higher incentive pay, litigation and a class-action settlement accrual, lifting it to 26.6% of revenue from 25.5% [1]. Operating income grew 5%, slower than revenue, so operating margin fell to 18.0% from 18.3%, and remains well below the 20.6% reached in 2022 [1].

Below the operating line the picture improved. Net interest and other expense fell $31.3 million, lifting net margin to 10.9% from 10.6% [1]. Diluted EPS rose 10% to $5.32, slightly faster than net income growth of 9%, as diluted shares fell to 124.1 million from 124.9 million [1]. Diluted EPS is still below the $5.65 reported in 2022 [1]. Cash generation was strong: operating cash flow reached $1,615.7 million, up $291.2 million, and capital expenditure fell to $481.4 million, leaving free cash flow of $1,134.3 million [1]. Working capital contributed $117.1 million in 2025 against $21.9 million in 2024, a gain of about $95 million (our calculation) that may not repeat [1][2].

Forward estimates show a return to growth on a normalized basis. Consensus expects FY2026 revenue of $6,666.1 million (+9.7%) and EPS of $8.50, and FY2027 revenue of $7,072.9 million (+6.1%) and EPS of $9.46 [3]. These consensus EPS figures are normalized and are not directly comparable with the $5.32 GAAP diluted EPS reported for 2025 [1][3]. Next-year EPS consensus fell 6.3% over the past 90 days, an early sign that analysts see the mortgage slowdown weighing on earnings [3]. Reported quarterly EPS beat consensus in each of the last four quarters, by between 1.8% and 9.7% [3]. These consensus figures are dated after the 10-K.
risk_assessment:
The filing names three principal risks: cybersecurity, regulatory and legal exposure, and economic sensitivity [1]. Cybersecurity carries the most documented consequences. The 2017 breach led to the July 2019 Consumer Settlement, which became effective on January 11, 2022 and requires third-party assessments of the security program [1]. The company lost certain key certifications, and customers paused business, forcing significant remediation spending that the filing does not quantify [1]. It also says its insurance may not be adequate for future losses, and that cloud migration to third-party hosts may expose it to new threats [1].

Regulatory exposure is wide and hard to size. The CFPB can seek civil money penalties of up to $1.0 million per day for known violations, and GDPR fines can reach 4% of annual worldwide turnover, although the company's turnover is not stated in the filing [1]. The filing describes the Consumer Settlement obligations as extensive, and AI regulation is multiplying, with the company noting that its use of AI in credit decisioning could draw enhanced scrutiny [1]. Economic sensitivity is the third risk: management expects U.S. mortgage credit activity in 2026 to be below 2025 levels, and refinancing activity is tied to interest rates [1]. International operations account for 23% of revenue, and the company generally does not mitigate currency risk [1].

The balance sheet adds a funding risk. The current ratio fell to 0.61x from 0.75x, the working capital deficit widened to $923.2 million, and debt due within twelve months rose to $1,038.0 million against $180.8 million of cash [1][2]. Debt to equity rose to 1.11x from 1.04x [1]. Free cash flow of $1,134.3 million covered the $232.8 million dividend, but buybacks of $927.5 million exceeded the residual cash flow and were partly funded by $474.7 million of commercial paper [1]. The Altman Z-score of 3.32 sits in the safe zone, and the Beneish M-score of -2.84 shows no manipulation warning, although the Altman model is designed for manufacturers and is less reliable for this business [2]. The Piotroski score of 8 of 9 failed only on the current ratio test [2]. Asia Pacific goodwill headroom is thin, so weaker cash flows there could trigger an impairment [1].
competitors_analysis:
We chose three peers from the candidate list. TransUnion (TRU) is the closest business model, a consumer credit reporting agency with two segments [4]. Paychex (PAYX) is the nearest match for the Workforce Solutions payroll and HR business, and it is similar in size at 1.0x Equifax's revenue [4]. Verisk (VRSK) is a data-analytics company serving insurance clients and is the smallest of the set at 0.5x Equifax's revenue [4]. FICO and ADP were excluded: FICO's scoring-software model differs from Equifax's data-bureau model, and ADP is 3.4 times Equifax's revenue [4].

Growth and valuation diverge. Equifax's 2025 revenue growth of 6.9% trails TransUnion's 9.4%, is roughly level with Verisk's 6.6%, and is ahead of Paychex's 5.6% [4]. On EV/EBITDA, Equifax trades at 16.92x, against TransUnion's 14.31x, Verisk's 20.18x and Paychex's 24.22x [4]. The premium to TransUnion is hard to justify on the operating data, since TransUnion has the higher EBITDA margin and faster growth [4]. Equifax's advantage lies in returns and cash: ROIC of 8.5% beats TransUnion's 6.7%, and free cash flow rose from $133 million in 2022 to $1,134 million in 2025 [4]. Consensus rates the stock a buy with a $205.10 target price [3].

Two caveats matter. The reported FCF conversion figure for Equifax (1.72) does not reconcile with FCF divided by EBITDA (about 0.62) using the same table, so any claim of cash-flow leadership should be verified against the filing before use [4]. Consensus EPS figures are normalized, so they should not be compared directly with peers' GAAP results without a like-for-like check [3][4]. On the operating evidence, Equifax is a mid-pack growth company with a strong cash trend but not the highest margins, and its premium to TransUnion needs support from a margin recovery in 2026 [4].

investment_theses.thesis: USIS margin expansion persists through the 2026 mortgage slowdown, because product pricing and diversified growth offset lower credit inquiry volumes.
investment_theses.evidence: USIS revenue rose 10% to $2,078.5 million and operating income rose 18% to $475.2 million, with margin at 22.9% versus 21.4% [1].
investment_theses.signpost: USIS operating margin at or above 22% in each quarterly report through Q1 2027.
investment_theses.invalidation: USIS margin falls below 21.4% in any quarter through Q1 2027, or mortgage pricing gains reverse.

investment_theses.thesis: Workforce Solutions remains the profit anchor even as U.S. mortgage activity falls in 2026.
investment_theses.evidence: Segment margin rose to 44.2% from 43.3%, operating income rose 8% to $1,141.5 million, and Verification Services grew 8% to $2,179.8 million [1].
investment_theses.signpost: Verification Services revenue growth of at least 5% reported in the Q1 2027 quarterly report.
investment_theses.invalidation: Verification Services revenue growth turns negative, or Workforce Solutions margin falls below 43%.

investment_theses.thesis: At $185.68 the shares price in faster growth than history supports, so the stock needs re-acceleration to earn its cost of capital.
investment_theses.evidence: The reverse DCF implies 12.4% annual revenue growth over ten years against a 5.8% historical three-year CAGR, and an implied IRR of 7.8% against an 11.2% WACC [2][3]. Consensus growth is 9.7% for FY2026 and 6.1% for FY2027 [3].
investment_theses.signpost: FY2026 reported revenue growth of at least 9%, shown in the FY2026 annual filing expected around February 2027.
investment_theses.invalidation: FY2026 revenue growth below 7%, or FY2027 EPS consensus cut below $9.00 in any quarter of 2027.

investment_theses.thesis: Debt due within twelve months is refinanced without strain, so the liquidity squeeze does not force cuts to buybacks or dividends.
investment_theses.evidence: Current debt of $1,038.0 million compares with cash of $180.8 million and a 0.61x current ratio, while free cash flow of $1,134.3 million covered the $232.8 million dividend but not the $927.5 million of buybacks in addition [1][2].
investment_theses.signpost: The FY2026 annual filing shows the current debt refinanced or repaid, with cash and revolver capacity above the remaining maturities.
investment_theses.invalidation: Commercial paper access is restricted, a ratings downgrade occurs, or buybacks are cut below the dividend level to conserve cash.
